newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: South Africa's Stals says lower rates possible.
newsitem.headline: South Africa's Stals says lower rates possible.

text.p: Chris Stals, governor of the South African Reserve Bank, said it was quite possible that interest rates would decline later this year in light of the recent economic slowdown.

Stals also told Reuters Financial Television that he did not think it was unrealistic to assume that South Africa would reach the government's 1997 target for 2.5 percent growth in the Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
"I think 2.5 percent is still possible," Stals said at the annual meeting of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) late Sunday.
Stals said economists had speculated that interest rates would decline in the second half of the year and he could also speculate along those lines.
"Against a backdrop of a slowdown in real economic activity in the last six months, it is quite possible that interest rates will decline later this year," Stals said.

In the first quarter of 1997 the GDP declined 1.0 percent from the fourth quarter of 1996, but Stals said this was due to adverse climatic conditions, which had lead to a 34 percent drop in agricultural production.
Manufacturing, however, showed growth of 3.6 percent for a year-on-year overall GDP growth of around 2.5 percent, Stals said.

Stals also said he was not overly concerned with expected capital outflows that were likely to follow a lifting on restrictions for private investors to transfer a limited amount of money out of the country on July 1.
He said there would probably be some "emotional reaction and for sentimental resons some people may want to have a nest-egg outside" the country.

But people who really had wanted to transfer money out of South Africa had probably already done it illegally and restrictions on transfers for corporate purposes and for institutional investors had already been lifted.
"Whatever private individuals want to transfer should be available in foreign exchange reserves," Stals said.
He noted that South Africa had some 22 billion rand in reserves, commercial banks had three to four billion and the Reserve Bank had credit lines of 15 billion, amounting to a total of 37 billion.
"I think if private investors want to transfer four to five billion out of the country that would be a substantial amount," Stals said.
Stals said that interest rates in South Africa were not "extremely high" when compared with other countries and long- term rates were actually the same as in the U.S., when adjusted for inflation.
"Short-term rates are higher, but that is because of inflation expectations," he said, adding:

"It's the yield curve that is wrong in South Africa, not the level of interest rates. Short term rates are well above long- term rates because people think inflation will go up before coming down again," Stals said.
The reserve bank's interest rate policy is dictated by changes in financial aggregates rather than changes in the real economy, Stals added.
"We must wait for financial activites also to reflect the slowdown, otherwise we create the stop-and-go policies of the 1960s and 1970s boom and bust," he said, adding:
"The interest rate level in South Africa will reflect changes in financial conditions and not so much changes in the real economy," Stals said.
((-- Peter Nielsen, Zurich Editorial +41 1 631 7340))
